walkthroughs.body_html:
Globalisation & Migration — a core area of GCSE Geography.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Globalisation & Migration brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Globalisation & Migration.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Roughly what % of Japan's population is over 65?
What does a wide-based pyramid show?
options: Ageing population
Youthful population
Decline
Stability

mcqs.q: Why do people move from rural to urban areas in LICs?
options: Because the government forces them to move to cities.
Because cities in poor countries are always better than the countryside.
A combination of push factors (rural poverty, lack of services, agricultural change) and pull factors (perceived jobs, education, healthcare) — though reality often disappoints.
Push factors are physical and pull factors are economic.

mcqs.q: Why do TNCs locate production in LICs?
options: Lower labour costs, weaker regulation, access to raw materials, large potential markets, and government incentives like tax breaks in special economic zones.
Because TNCs want to develop poorer countries and lift them out of poverty.
Because LICs have better infrastructure than HICs.
Because the government forces them to move to cities.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between push and pull factors in migration?
options: Because LICs have better infrastructure than HICs.
Push and pull factors are the same thing.
Push factors are physical and pull factors are economic.
Push factors drive people away from their origin (war, poverty, persecution, disaster); pull factors attract people to a destination (jobs, safety, family, healthcare, education).
